message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions (e.g., unpaid rent, damage beyond normal wear). | • Get a written receipt and keep a copy of the lease.
• Take photos of the unit before moving in and after moving out. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to maintain the premises in a safe, sanitary, and livable condition.
• Repairs for health and safety issues must be made promptly. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may withhold rent or seek a repair‑and‑deduct remedy (though this is limited in Texas). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Keep records of all payments (bank statements, receipts). | | **Entry Rights** | • Landlords must give at least 24‑hour written notice before entering, except in emergencies.
• Notice must specify the time and purpose. | • Ask for a written notice if you suspect the landlord is entering without proper notice. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the federal Fair Housing Act and Texas’ own Fair Housing Act, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a month‑to‑month lease with 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the landlord must provide a valid reason for early termination (e.g., non‑payment, violation of lease). | • Keep a copy of the lease and any notices. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment), file a lawsuit, and obtain a court order.
• Eviction cannot be carried out without a court order. | • If you receive an eviction notice, respond promptly and consider seeking legal counsel. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • Texas law does not allow tenants to withhold rent for repairs (unlike some other states). | • Instead, you can request repairs in writing and, if the landlord fails to act, you may pursue a repair‑and‑deduct claim in small‑claims court. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords cannot monitor your activities inside the unit (e.g., no hidden cameras). | • Report any suspicious monitoring to the police or a tenant‑rights group. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities.
• If utilities are included, the landlord must maintain the service. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Subletting** | • Subletting is allowed only if the lease permits it or the landlord consents in writing. | • Get written permission before subletting. | | **Dispute Resolution** | • Many leases include a mediation or arbitration clause.
• If disputes arise, you can seek mediation through local tenant‑rights groups or the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs. | • Keep all correspondence and document any disputes. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand the terms, notice periods, and responsibilities. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and payment records. 3. **Know the Law** – Familiarize yourself with the Texas Property Code sections relevant to tenancy. 4. **Communicate in Writing** – Whenever possible, use email or certified mail. 5. **Seek Help Early** – If you face a problem, contact a local tenant‑rights organization (e.g., Texas Tenants Union, local legal aid). ### Resources - **Texas Property Code** – Sections 92.001–92.021 cover landlord‑tenant rights. - **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** – Offers resources and a hotline. - **U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)** – For fair housing complaints. - **Local Legal Aid** – Many counties have free or low‑cost legal assistance for tenants. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is for general educational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. For advice tailored to your specific situation, consult a licensed attorney or a qualified tenant‑rights advocate.
